messages.subject: Q&A is there a way for mlg.id to ignore NA and/or allow for x mismatches?
messages.subject_clean: Q&A is there a way for mlg.id to ignore NA and/or allow for x mismatches?
messages.body_plain:
Hi everyone,

I have used the mlg.id <http://mlg.id> function to identify individuals that were sampled multiple times (duplicates in the data) in the following way:

cloned_gt <- mlg.id <http://mlg.id>(df)

duplicates <- cloned_gt[which(lengths(cloned_gt)>1)]

But this will only find exact matches. Is there a way to ignore NAs in the data? So that for example genotype A B C D and genotype A B NA D would be considered a match?

In addition to this, would it be possible to allow for 1 (or more) mismatches? So that genotype A B C D would be considered a match with A B E D?

Any help would be greatly appreciated!

All the best,
Anneke

messages.subject: Re: Q&A is there a way for mlg.id to ignore NA and/or allow for x mismatches?
messages.subject_clean: Q&A is there a way for mlg.id to ignore NA and/or allow for x mismatches?
messages.body_plain:
Hi Anneke,

All of what you are asking is indeed possible in poppr! I would suggest you read the "mlg" poppr vignette. You can access it by typing in the R console:

```
library(poppr)
vignette(topic = "mlg", package = "poppr")
```

I will use the monpop dataset which is included with poppr to quickly demonstrate how you can do what you are asking (but you should definitely also read the appropriate vignette in order to see all options and understand the topic)

Is there a way to ignore NAs in the data?

All we need to do is use the mlg.filter function with a genetic distance of our choice. I will use the diss.dist function to calculate distances between genotypes, as it has the desired property that each unit is equal to one allele difference. By setting the distance threshold for separating genotypes to 0 + a very tiny number, poppr will ignore missing data and consider individuals with the same genotype apart from missing data as matches.

```
data(monpop)
mlg.filter(monpop, distance = diss.dist) <- 0 + .Machine$double.eps^0.5
monpop
```

Similarly if you would like to allow 1 missmatch (or more), all you have to do is supply the appropriate distance threshold:

```
mlg.filter(monpop, distance = diss.dist) <- 1 + .Machine$double.eps^0.5
monpop
```

Hope this helps
Nikos

messages.subject: alleles set to zero with genind2genalex
messages.subject_clean: alleles set to zero with genind2genalex
messages.body_plain:
Dear all,
I am having some issues with converting a genlight object to a genalex file... My genind object was imported as a VcfR with the option return.alleles=TRUE. It includes 111 individuals, 1808 loci (2612 alleles). There are some missing genotypes coded as NAs; individuals that are homozygous for an allele score as 2 for that allele, and heterozygous score as 1 (for two alleles), and missing genotypes as NA.
When I convert it to the genalex format using genind2genalex, however, all alleles are set to zero.
Has anyone encountered this issue?

messages.subject: Re: [poppr] alleles set to zero with genind2genalex
messages.subject_clean: [poppr] alleles set to zero with genind2genalex
messages.body_plain:
Hello,

If only missing genotypes are converted to zero, that's normal, but if ALL genotypes are converted to zero, then there is likely a bug.

I have a couple of questions that may help narrow down what is happening:

1. If you try to convert a subset of your data  (e.g. 5 individuals over three loci), do you still see zeroes for alleles?
2. If you answered yes to the above question, what happens when you run genind2df() on that subset of data? Do you also get zeroes for the alleles?

All the best,
Zhian

messages.subject: Pairwise Amova
messages.body_plain:
Hello again,
I am working with 3 populations and, to explore the genetic structure among and between populations, I performed an AMOVA using poppr.amova, which also provide a PhI-stat.

Now, I was wondering how can I do this pairwise, to determine which pair of populations pair is the most differentiated and obtain a pairwise index of population differentiation PHI-pt.

I guess, I can subset my dataset and perform the AMOVA by pair, but I'm not sure this is the most appropriate way to do this.

Again, many thanks

RV

messages.subject: Re: [poppr] Pairwise Amova
messages.body_plain:
At the moment, there is no feature to do this automatically in part because it gets complex when you introduce hierarchy into the mix.

There are alternatives that you might try that would give you the same kind of information you are looking for:

1. Create a bootstrapped tree from distances between populations using aboot(data, ~pop) (https://grunwaldlab.github.io/poppr/reference/aboot.html)

2. Use DAPC to create a visualization showing how the populations relate to each other in 2-D space (https://raw.githubusercontent.com/thibautjombart/adegenet/master/tutorials/tutorial-dapc.pdf)

3. If you have diploid data, you can also calculate pairwise Fst via the {hierfstat} package https://www.rdocumentation.org/packages/hierfstat/versions/0.5-7/topics/pairwise.neifst https://www.rdocumentation.org/packages/hierfstat/versions/0.5-7/topics/pairwise.WCfst

Hope that helps.

Best,
Zhian

messages.subject: Re: [poppr] Pairwise Amova
messages.body_plain:
I don't think it's terribly necessary. The DAPC shows visually what the AMOVA is doing (albiet, using a slightly different method of input data). Doing a pairwise AMOVA would only reduce your degrees of freedom and won't really tell you anything new.

We used DAPC to bolster the AMOVA results for our analyses back in 2017: "When we analyze the AMOVA results in light of the DAPC results (Fig. 5 <https://peerj.com/articles/4152/#fig-5>), it becomes clear that the regional patterns of differentiation are largely driven by isolates from Mexico and CA." (https://peerj.com/articles/4152/).

Best,
Zhian
